The University Center for Human Values invites applications for Laurance S. Rockefeller Visiting Faculty Fellowships for the academic year 2027-28. Fellows devote an academic year in residence at Princeton to research and writing about topics involving human values in public and private life. This full-time visiting program is open to scholars in all disciplines across the humanities and social sciences. We welcome applications from scholars from a variety of disciplines.

Fellows are expected to reside in or around Princeton or demonstrate to the program's satisfaction the ability to commute to campus on a daily basis during the 12-week fall and spring semesters. Fellows pursue their own research and are active contributors to the intellectual life of the Center. This includes participating in a weekly seminar attended by fellows and Center faculty to discuss work in progress and in various other seminars, colloquia and lectures sponsored by the Center. Fellows enjoy access to Firestone Library and to a wide range of activities and facilities throughout the University.

The fellowship extends from September 1 to June 1. Fellows receive a stipend paid in nine equal installments. Ordinarily, home institutions provide a portion of their salaries in addition to benefits, although this is not a requirement. Independent scholars are eligible to apply.

Main considerations in the evaluation of applications are the following:

 The significance of the proposed research and its relevance to the purposes of the University Center for Human Values 
 The quality of a candidate’s previous research and the contribution the candidate is likely to make in the future through their scholarship
The likelihood that the research would benefit from being conducted in the University Center environment

Qualifications

Candidates must have a doctorate or equivalent professional degree and a strong record of research publications appropriate to their career stage. Typically, Fellows hold faculty positions at other universities or colleges; in exceptional cases, we consider applications from independent scholars when there is a high level of scholarly achievement. This is not a postdoctoral fellowship program, and we do not generally consider candidates who will have held the Ph.D. for less than two years at the time of appointment, or who are coming directly from a postdoctoral fellowship.

Application Instructions

Candidates must submit an online application: https://apply.interfolio.com/189111.

Required materials:

 A CV
 One scholarly paper (no more than 12,000 words) written in the past three years
 A statement (no more than 1,500 words) describing the proposed research project, including a brief working title for the project
 Contact information for three referees, including at least one referee who was not a graduate advisor (note that referees will be asked to send in their letters fairly quickly – by October 22, 2026, for best consideration).

Applicant materials must be submitted by the deadline: October 15, 2026, 11:59 p.m. EST. We aim to announce decisions by late March 2027.

Description
The Kenneth C. Griffin Department of Economics at the University of Chicago invites applications for a full-time Research Associate for a three-year term starting in the 2026-2027 academic year. 

About the TMW Center
Co-directed by Dana Suskind (Biological Sciences Division), and John List (Economics), the TMW Center for Early Learning + Public Health aspires to create a population-level shift in the knowledge and behavior of parents and caregivers to optimize the foundational brain development in children, birth to five years of age, particularly those born into poverty. The TMW Center has conducted 12 randomized controlled, quasi-experimental, and implementation trials to date and plans to continue its active randomized controlled and implementation trials, including ongoing data collection and analysis in the coming years.  As part of these research projects, the Center is continuing to adapt and validate two state-of-the-art tools: (1) the SPEAK - a computer-adaptive tool designed to assess caretaker expectations and knowledge of early childhood cognitive and language development, and (2) the Luet – a wearable device paired with an app that uses machine learning to measure early child development through language and physical movement.

Job Summary:
The Research Associate will work, in partnership with Co-Director Suskind and Senior Research Associate Pernaudet, to design and execute TMW Center research projects. Core responsibilities include conducting rigorous quantitative analyses, writing and publishing findings, presenting research, and leading grant applications in collaboration with Professors List and Suskind. The position entails collaboration on new and ongoing research projects, with a highly interdisciplinary team of economists, psychologists, engineers, app developers, and more. A primary focus of the work is applying economic models and machine learning techniques to empirical analysis of data generated from TMW Center’s research projects, including via Luet and the SPEAK.

The position will also allow the Research Associate to be part of the vibrant research environment of the TMW Center for Early Learning + Public Health and the Kenneth C. Griffin Department of Economics at The University of Chicago.  This position will report to the TMW Center Co-Directors, Dana Suskind and John List, with additional reporting to the Center COO for matters outside of research. This position will require a commitment of at least 3 years.

This position is benefits-eligible. The University of Chicago offers a wide range of benefits programs and resources for eligible employees, including health, retirement, and paid time off. Information about the benefit offerings can be found in the Benefits Guidebook.

	Superior interpersonal skills and the ability to work effectively with a wide range of individuals and constituencies in a diverse professional environment required.
	Ability to effectively manage a heavy workload, competing priorities, and tight deadlines required.

	Ability to work both independently and as a team member required.

Qualifications

	Applicants must have a Ph.D. in Economics.

	A microeconomist with experience in experimental and behavioral economics is preferred

Position
1-3 full-time Post-Doctoral Associate positions, available starting in 2027 for 1-3 years (one-year positions are only available to applicants who have secured a subsequent appointment as an assistant professor, research scientist, or research economist)

Employer MIT FutureTech (futuretech.mit.edu) at:

MIT Sloan School of Management’s Initiative on the Digital Economy (IDE) and
MIT Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Lab (CSAIL)

Location
Cambridge, Massachusetts, USA

Job Description
Dr. Neil Thompson, Director of MIT FutureTech, seeks to hire up to three Postdoctoral Associates, with a preference for candidates whose research connects to at least one of the following areas:

(i)	AI progress and timelines
Rapid advances in AI capabilities have raised both excitement and uncertainty about the pace of future progress. Projections of when specific milestones (e.g., human level performance on complex tasks, widespread deployment of autonomous systems) will be reached differ significantly across researchers, research fields, and industry. This project area seeks to rigorously characterize historical and current trends in AI development and to model plausible future trajectories. Relevant work might include: quantitative measurement of scaling laws and other empirical regularities in algorithmic improvement; analysis of hardware, energy, data, and talent constraints that could accelerate or limit progress; economic, regulatory, and geopolitical factors shaping investment and research concentration; scenario modeling of short-, medium, and long term capability benchmarks; and assessment of feedback loops between AI deployment and further innovation. Insights generated should help clarify realistic timelines, identify key uncertainties, and inform strategic decisions by firms, governments, and society at large regarding preparedness and governance of advanced AI systems. Examples of previous work from the lab in this area include: Algorithmic Progress; Last Mile.

(ii)	The Effect of AI on Science 
AI has driven advancements in many scientific fields, such as drug discovery, materials science, protein folding, or weather prediction. It is also well known that scientific progress is a key engine for economic growth. This project focuses on understanding the impact of AI on science and the resulting economic consequences. Key topics we aim to address include quantifying the impact of AI on scientific progress and economic growth, the extent to which AI will augment and/or change the R&D production function, and the implications of AI-driven R&D for researchers, firms, and policy. Examples of previous work from the lab in this area include: Influence of Industry; AI-augmented R&D.

(iii)	Future of Work and the Labor Market Effects of AI and ICT
What are the (global) labor market implications of new technologies, such as AI and ICT? Do workers within firms benefit from IT improvements and the adoption of AI? If so, which workers specifically benefit, and which are adversely affected through slower wage growth or job displacement? How quickly will jobs be replaced or augmented by AI? Are workers (or individual tasks) complements or substitutes to AI and ICT? Furthermore, how does overall labor demand change in response to advancements in AI? We aim to address these and related questions by leveraging detailed firm-worker-level data from administrative sources (e.g., census data), publicly available task-level data (e.g., ONET), and self-collected surveys. By studying these dynamics, our goal is to gain a deeper understanding of the future of work in the context of the rise of new technologies. Examples of previous work from the lab in this area include: Beyond AI Exposure; Expertise; Crashing waves vs. Rising Tides.

(iv)	The Impact of AI on Industry and Firm Performance 
AI is widely recognized as having the potential to revolutionize industries and transform firms’ production processes. However, significant gaps remain in our understanding of how AI will affect firm and industry performance both within and across countries. In this project, we aim to develop novel measures of industry exposure to AI and compile data on AI adoption to investigate how AI shapes firm performance, productivity, and market power in national and international contexts. Key questions include identifying the key determinants of AI adoption; how AI affects firms’ market shares and productivity; how these changes influence competition and aggregate productivity; and whether cross-country differences in AI adoption and exposure will narrow or widen existing economic disparities. Examples of the lab’s previous work in this area include: IT and RTS. 

In addition to researching these issues, the post-doc will be expected to become a team leader, supervising and mentoring younger students. 
 
Qualifications
•	PhD or equivalent in economics or related field
•	Demonstrated expertise in computing / AI 
•	Interest in working in an interdisciplinary lab with computer scientists and engineers
•	Strong data analysis skills, including statistical/econometric training
•	For some positions, experience working with U.S. census data would be a plus
•	Knowledge of relevant theoretical models
•	Proficiency with a modern programming language, e.g., Python, R
•	Solid English communication skills (verbal and written)
•	Desire and skill (e.g. organizational abilities) to work in teams


The post-doc’s primary appointment would be at the MIT Sloan School of Management, and would have a secondary appointment at the MIT Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Lab.

Salary
$73,308 - $90,000 per year, plus benefits.

To apply  
Submit the following materials via the AEA platform no later than November 15th:
(i)	CV
(ii)	Job market paper (or other sample of previous research)
(iii)	Three letters of reference 
(iv)	Cover letter discussing the applicant’s experience and which research projects would be of interest

Selected candidates will be interviewed via Zoom.

About MIT FutureTech
Led by Dr. Neil Thompson, MIT FutureTech is an interdisciplinary group of computer scientists, engineers, and economists who study the foundations of progress in computing and Artificial Intelligence: the trends, implications, opportunities, and risks. FutureTech is one of the largest research groups at MIT. It sits both within the Computer Science and AI Lab and the Sloan School of Management.  A distinctive strength of our lab is access to a large set of rich and unique data sources that allow us to study the economics of AI and computing. We collaborate extensively with major government agencies and industry leaders. Our work is supported by a broad range of partners, including, among many others, Open Philanthropy, the National Science Foundation, Google, Microsoft, Accenture, IBM, Amazon, and Los Alamos National Lab.

About Dr. Neil Thompson, the Director of MIT FutureTech - futuretech.mit.edu/team/neil-thompson 
Dr. Thompson is the Director of MIT FutureTech. Before starting FutureTech, Dr. Thompson was a professor of Innovation and Strategy at the MIT Sloan School of Management.  His PhD is in Business & Public Policy from Berkeley.  He also holds Master’s degrees in: Computer Science (Berkeley), Economics (London School of Economics), and Statistics (Berkeley).  Before joining academia, Dr. Thompson was a management consultant with Bain & Company and worked for the Canadian Government and the United Nations.

The Council of Economic Advisers (CEA) seeks a Senior Economist in labor economics for a one-year appointment beginning as soon as possible, with the possibility of extension.

CEA was established by the Employment Act of 1946 to provide the President with objective economic analysis and advice. Senior Economists are the core of the Council's professional staff. Each holds a substantive portfolio, writes directly for the Council's Members, and represents CEA in the interagency policy process.

The labor portfolio typically includes:
 Assessment of labor market conditions, including pre-release review of BLS data and preparation of materials briefing the President and senior White House staff on the monthly Employment Situation report
 The labor market components of the Administration's macroeconomic forecast — employment, unemployment, participation, hours, compensation, and productivity — developed jointly with Treasury and OMB
 Authorship of chapters and original analysis for the Economic Report of the President
 Policy analysis and interagency representation on labor supply, immigration and the workforce, education and training, unemployment insurance, occupational licensing, labor standards, and care infrastructure
 Review of proposed regulations and legislative proposals with material labor market consequences
 Representation of the United States in international fora, including OECD working parties

Qualifications 
PhD in economics or a closely related field, ideally with an established research record in labor economics. Strong applied econometric skills, facility with large survey and administrative microdata, and the ability to produce rigorous analysis on short deadlines and explain it clearly to non-economists. Tenured and tenure-track faculty on leave and economists at research institutions are especially encouraged to apply; CEA has a long tradition of one-year appointments of this kind, and prior CEA service is common among leading labor economists.

CEA's usefulness to the President rests on the quality and integrity of its analysis, and the Council's work is held to professional research standards.

U.S. citizenship; favorable background investigation; financial disclosure and compliance with executive branch ethics rules, which may require divestiture or recusal from consulting and other outside activities. Position is located in Washington, DC and is not remote-eligible.

The Center for the Future of Cities (CFC) at Tecnológico de Monterrey invites applications for a tenure-track position in Urban Economics. We seek candidates completing their Ph.D. by Summer 2027, as well as postdoctoral researchers and early-career faculty, interested in building a research agenda on open questions with direct relevance for urban policy in Latin America.
Tecnológico de Monterrey is the largest private university in Mexico and among the most highly regarded in Latin America. It is making a major investment to become a leading research university in the region. Within this context, the CFC is an interdisciplinary research center that brings together economists, data scientists, and urban planners under a shared premise: rigorous research should inform not only the academic literature but also the governance of cities. The Center maintains formal collaborations with municipal and metropolitan planning agencies, and its projects are designed to produce both peer-reviewed publications and measurable influence on public policy.

What We Offer
Access to rich and granular datasets for Mexican metropolitan areas, much of it new to academic research.
Direct engagement with policy: projects are developed with government agencies, and findings reach both decision-makers and academic outlets.
Protected time for publication: teaching is one class per term in the Department of Economics (joint appointment), defined by the candidate's profile.
Collaboration with an interdisciplinary team working on urban simulation, land use, and transport modeling.
Internationally competitive compensation according to career stage.
Research funds, cloud computing infrastructure, and active collaborations with partner universities in North and Latin America.
Room to develop an independent research agenda, contribute to large-scale applied projects, and build and lead a team.
Research areas of interest
Affordable housing models and housing production.
Impacts of land-use regulation on housing costs.
Property tax and municipal public finance.
Infrastructure and fiscal costs of urban expansion and sprawl.
Effects of transportation systems on land values.
Spatial and general equilibrium models of land, zoning, and taxation.

Qualifications
Candidates should have strong quantitative training and demonstrated experience in urban economics, spatial analysis, econometrics, or general equilibrium modeling. A strong publication pipeline, or clear potential for high-impact publishing, is highly valued. Working proficiency in Spanish is required.
Early applications are encouraged: submissions will be reviewed on a rolling basis, and Zoom interviews will be scheduled as strong candidates are identified. Candidates who advance will deliver an online job talk. Finalists will be invited to an in-person campus visit.

jp_full_text:
The La Follette School of Public Affairs (LFS) seeks to hire a scholar whose research examines how market-based institutions, competitive structures, and incentive-compatible policy design can address major societal challenges. The successful candidate will conduct theoretically grounded and empirically rigorous research on the role of markets in domains traditionally shaped by public policy, regulation, or collective action problems.

We are particularly interested in scholars who analyze how prices, property rights, competition, decentralized information, and institutional design affect outcomes in areas such as:

Education/school finance and school choice
Financial regulation and capital markets
Housing supply and land-use reform
Technology policy and innovation markets
Transportation and infrastructure finance
International trade and tariffs
State and local economic development
Climate and environmental policy (e.g., carbon pricing, cap-and-trade systems)
Energy markets and grid reform
Agricultural policy and food systems

The candidate may be an economist, political scientist, public policy scholar, legal scholar, or affiliated social scientist whose work engages deeply with the economic logic of markets and institutional design. We welcome scholars using diverse methodological approaches, including structural modeling, reduced-form econometrics, field experiments, institutional analysis, and political economy frameworks.

The successful candidate will contribute to teaching in public policy analysis, microeconomics for policy, regulatory policy, and sector-specific policy courses. They will strengthen LFS’s capacity to train students to evaluate when markets succeed, when they fail, how policy can improve their functioning, and how government failure represents an omnipresent risk.

They will contribute to an environment that fosters engagement and a sense of belonging for faculty, staff, students and members of the broader community.

The successful candidate, as a member of the College of L&S, will proactively contribute to, support, and advance the college’s commitment to excellence among all aspects of their teaching, mentoring, research, and service.

In the College of Letters & Science, we provide a liberal arts education that is both broad and deep through excellent, empathic teaching. We hire faculty who are interested in pursuing difficult questions, making new discoveries, and making an impact in their field. The Defense Analysis Department at the Naval Postgraduate School, Monterey, California, is seeking to fill a tenure-track position, open as to rank, in Security Studies.  
NPS takes teaching and research seriously, and candidates must show a strong commitment to graduate education and scholarship. The candidate will teach mid-career military officers and civilians from special operations and information operations organizations across all branches and services of the U.S. Armed Forces and allied countries and advise graduate theses. NPS follows a quarter system, and the normal teaching workload is four graduate courses per year.

Candidates must demonstrate the ability to pursue an independent program of innovative, high-quality research in areas such as national and international security, future warfare, conflict studies, terrorism, insurgency, political violence, artificial intelligence and conflict, innovation, or strategic decision-making. The candidate must have an interest in interdisciplinary research and willingness to work with a cross-disciplinary faculty and military and policy stakeholders. 

The Defense Analysis Department (DA) provides the critical thinking and analytical skills necessary for national security leaders to deal with the complexities and challenges of current and future operating and strategic environments. DA offers an M.S. in Defense Analysis with degree tracks in special operations and irregular warfare, applied design for innovation, and information strategy and political warfare, along with graduate certificates in social network analysis and special operations and regional governance. Home to 150 in-residence graduate students, forty members of a cross-disciplinary teaching and research faculty, and five research centers (high-performance computing lab, social network analysis lab, regional affairs and terrorism research center, information strategy center, and a maker space). DA faculty publish in top journals (e.g., American Political Science Review, Journal of Military History), university book presses (e.g., Cambridge and Chicago) and policy outlets (e.g. War on the Rocks, The Conversation), receive fellowships (e.g., Fullbright, Guggenheim), obtain external funding (e.g., DOD, NSF), earn association scholarship awards (e.g., Society for Military History, American Political Science Association), are recognized for teaching excellence, and work directly with US and global national security leaders. 

Additional information about our programs and faculty can be found at Welcome - Department of Defense Analysis - Naval Postgraduate School. 
The Naval Postgraduate School (NPS) provides graduate education to more than 1,500 resident and 1,000 online military officers of the uniformed services, Department of Defense civilians, and members of the international defense community. Most departments and programs are highly ranked, including the US News and World Report rated #1 Homeland Security Program. NPS is located on the central coast of California in Monterey. 

Minimum Qualifications: 
A Ph.D. degree in a relevant Social Science or Humanities discipline (e.g., History, Political Science, Economics, Strategic Studies, Public Policy, International Relations, Communications, Psychology, Sociology, Anthropology, Philosophy, Information Science, and other fields related to strategic studies). 
U.S. citizenship is required. Must be eligible for a security clearance. 
Publication records commensurate with academic experience. 


Salary is highly competitive and commensurate with qualifications and experience. Relocation expenses, including recruitment/relocation incentive, may be authorized in accordance with applicable regulations.

For more veterans’ preference information, visit: http://www.fedshirevets.gov/job/vetpref/index.aspx.

Position Summary

The Council of Economic Advisers seeks a Staff Economist to lead supply chain analysis across the nation's most critical and strategically vulnerable sectors. The role combines applied microeconomic and trade analysis with hands-on supply chain mapping—tracing where critical goods and their upstream inputs actually originate—and modeling how economic, trade, and procurement tools can shift sourcing toward the United States and partner nations.

The portfolio spans four priority areas: pharmaceuticals (finished drugs, active pharmaceutical ingredients (APIs), and key starting materials (KSMs)); semiconductors (with an emphasis on legacy/mature-node "foundational" chips); batteries and drones (cells, components, and the unmanned aircraft supply base); and critical minerals (extraction and, critically, processing and refining). A common analytical toolkit applies across all four: identify single-source vulnerabilities, distinguish direct from indirect exposure, and design economic levers to diversify supply.

This is a high-impact position for an economist who can move fluently between rigorous quantitative work and concrete policy design, and who is comfortable briefing senior officials on time-sensitive questions.
________________________________________

Key Responsibilities

Supply chain mapping and dependency analysis (across all priority sectors)

 Build and maintain an evidence base on where critical goods and their upstream inputs originate, identifying single-source and country-concentration risks.
 Distinguish extraction/assembly from the true chokepoints, which often sit midstream—e.g., mineral processing and refining, mature-node foundry capacity, cell and cathode/anode manufacturing, and API/KSM synthesis.
 Integrate data from customs and import records, HS/HTS-level trade flows, FDA establishment registrations, foundry capacity by node and geography, and commercial supply chain sources to quantify concentration (e.g., HHI, single-country shares) and map vulnerabilities.
 Develop criticality metrics (defense and clinical relevance, substitutability, shortage/disruption history) and resilience metrics (geographic diversification, domestic capacity, inventory, stockpiles).

Sector-specific focus areas

 Pharmaceuticals: finished-drug, API, and KSM sourcing; shortage risk.
 Semiconductors: legacy/mature-node chips embedded in autos, defense systems, medical devices, appliances, and grid hardware; risks from non-market capacity expansion and price suppression.
 Batteries and drones: lithium-ion cells and components, cathode/anode and precursor materials, and the unmanned aircraft (UAS) supply base, including secure-component and trusted-supplier considerations.
 Critical minerals: rare earths, lithium, cobalt, nickel, graphite, gallium, germanium and similar.

Policy tool analysis

 Model the cost, feasibility, and likely supply response of economic and procurement levers, including trade remedies, Buy American and domestic-content preferences and penalties, federal procurement preferences and restrictions, advance purchase and offtake commitments, stockpiling, and targeted onshoring/ally-shoring incentives.
 Estimate effects on prices, availability and shortage risk, domestic manufacturing investment, and downstream costs; assess budgetary impact, unintended consequences, and gaming risks.
 Conduct cost-benefit and trade-off analysis weighing resilience gains against consumer-price and fiscal effects.

Partner-country and friend-shoring strategy

 Analyze opportunities to diversify supply with allied and partner nations, including the economic case for ally-shoring of upstream production and processing.
 Assess how trade preferences, joint procurement, coordinated incentives, and partnership frameworks could stand up trusted alternative suppliers and shared stockpiles.

Briefing and inter-agency work

 Produce memos, charts, and briefing materials.
 Support inter-agency analysis with partners.
________________________________________

Qualifications

Required

 Advanced degree in economics or a closely related quantitative field (PhD preferred; exceptional candidates with a master's and strong relevant experience considered).
 Demonstrated applied skills in microeconomics, industrial organization, and/or international trade.
 Strong empirical and data skills (e.g., Stata, R, or Python) and the ability to work with messy real-world trade, customs, regulatory, and industry datasets.
 Ability to translate technical analysis into clear, decision-ready writing for non-economist principals.- Capacity to work quickly and accurately under deadline pressure on sensitive policy questions.

Preferred

 Familiarity with one or more priority sectors: pharmaceutical manufacturing and the API/KSM value chain; semiconductor manufacturing and the mature-node landscape; battery and UAS supply chains; or critical minerals extraction and processing.
 Knowledge of U.S. trade- and industrial-policy instruments.
 Experience with supply-chain, network, or concentration analysis.
 Prior government, think tank, or inter-agency experience.

Princeton University is pleased to announce the call for applications to the Fung Global Fellows Program at the Princeton Institute for International and Regional Studies (PIIRS). The program will select early-career scholars from around the world to be in residence at Princeton for an academic year and to engage in research and discussion around a common theme. The fellowships will be awarded to those employed outside the United States who have a faculty appointment or a professional research appointment, and they will be expected to return to their positions at the conclusion of the fellowship. 

Democratic governance faces mounting pressure around the world. The rise of populist movements, declining trust in institutions, polarization, disinformation, and democratic backsliding (including in democracies once considered as consolidated) have prompted renewed debate about whether democracy's ascendance in the late 20th century was more fragile than assumed. At the same time, democracies have proven resilient in unexpected ways through grassroots mobilization, institutional safeguards, judicial independence, and civic renewal, raising the question of what, precisely, allows some democratic systems to weather crisis while others erode or collapse.

During the 2027-28 academic year, the program theme will be "Democracy in Crisis?" We invite applications from scholars who study the challenges confronting democratic governance and/or the sources of democratic resilience. Projects might explore the drivers and dynamics of populism; the erosion of democratic norms and institutions; the role of media, technology, and disinformation in shaping political life; the relationship between economic inequality and democratic legitimacy; or the strategies through which citizens, civil society, and institutions have defended or renewed democratic practice. We are equally interested in work that interrogates the conceptual and normative foundations of democracy itself, what it means, who it serves, and how it has been imagined and contested across different political and cultural traditions.

Applicants may address any region of the world and can bring contemporary and/or historical perspectives to bear. We welcome scholars from across the humanities and social sciences.

Applicants must apply online at https://apply.interfolio.com/191685. Applications are due on November 16, 2026 (11:59 p.m. EST).

To be eligible, applicants must have received their Ph.D. (or equivalent) generally after September 1, 2017. Candidates who are currently enrolled in a Ph.D. program or employed as postdocs are not eligible to apply. Fellowships will be awarded on the strength of a candidate's proposed research project, the relationship of that project to the program's theme, the candidate's scholarly record, and their ability to contribute to the intellectual life of the program. For more information, see: https://funggfp.princeton.edu/applications.

The following items must be submitted by the applicant, in English, by November 16, 2026:

Cover letter (1.5 pages maximum)

Research proposal (maximum of 3 pages, single spaced)
One writing sample (article or book chapter, maximum of 50 pages)
The names and email addresses for three referees, who will be contacted automatically by the online application system with an invitation to upload their letter of recommendation to the system by the application deadline. 

Should an offer be made, successful candidates who hold faculty appointments or professional research appointments will be required to submit an official letter from their current employer affirming that they would be permitted to accept the offer and to spend the academic year at Princeton University.The work location for these positions is in-person, on campus at Princeton University.

The Department of Economics in the Williams School of Commerce, Economics, and Politics at Washington and Lee University invites applications from candidates with teaching and research interests in macroeconomics for a tenure-track position at the rank of assistant professor of Economics. The appointment will begin July 1, 2027.

The successful candidate will teach the department’s required macroeconomics courses (Principles of Macroeconomics and Macroeconomic Theory) and develop electives that build on existing departmental strengths while expanding opportunities for students.

Washington and Lee University is a highly selective, private, liberal arts college, located in Lexington, VA (population 7,000). W&L’s Economics department offers an undergraduate major in Economics and supports many interdisciplinary programs across campus. 

This position requires a strong commitment to excellence in teaching within an undergraduate liberal arts setting. Candidates should demonstrate the capacity to publish high-quality scholarly research. The university supports faculty research through a generous five-year sabbatical cycle, a pre-tenure research leave program, opportunities for summer salary support, travel stipends, and paid undergraduate research assistants. The department also hosts a seminar series that meets regularly throughout the academic year and features internal and external speakers.

The school calendar consists of two 13-week terms, one in the fall and one in the winter, along with our unique 4-week spring term. The regular teaching load is five courses per year. New hires teach a 2-2-0 load in their first year to provide an opportunity to fully participate in W&L’s New Faculty Cohort, a comprehensive, year-long faculty development program. 

The expected salary for this position is between $112,000- $118,000. Offers are based on factors such as relevant education, experience, tenure status, internal equity, and market and organizational considerations.

Washington and Lee University offers a generous and comprehensive benefits package designed to support the well-being of employees and their families, as well as substantial support for faculty development through research funding, a strong culture of mentorship, and a pre-tenure leave program. To learn more about working at W&L, employee benefits, and life in the Shenandoah Valley, visit jobs.wlu.edu.

Washington and Lee is an Equal Opportunity Employer seeking candidates committed to high standards of scholarship, performance, professionalism, and to a welcoming campus community. Job description requirements are representative, but not all‐inclusive of the knowledge, skill, and abilities needed to successfully perform this job. Reasonable accommodations may be made to enable qualified individuals with disabilities to perform essential functions.

jp_title: Weiss Fund Fellowship for Junior Researchers
jp_full_text:
The Weiss Fund Fellowship provides supplementary financial support for exceptional job market PhD candidates accepting positions in Weiss Fund-eligible countries and doing work aligned with the Weiss Fund's mission and objectives. The Fellowship award will be offered for a maximum of three years, with annual extensions based on performance evaluations at the end of every year.

Applicants are encouraged to seek and apply early to positions in Weiss-eligible countries, as receiving an offer from such a position is a core eligibility requirement. However, candidates do not need to have secured such a position at the time of application, and we encourage potential applicants with eligible jobs to apply for this fellowship as soon as possible. The fellowship is intended to support candidates for whom it is marginal to the decision to take a position in a Weiss-eligible country, that is, candidates weighing such a position against a competing option elsewhere.

Eligibility

Fellowships are awarded through a competitive selection process, with a limited number of offers. Applicants must be graduating from globally leading universities and fall into one of the following two categories:

Track 1:  Assistant Professor Positions

Applicants with Assistant Professor position offers at an academic institution in a Weiss-eligible country. These are countries with a per capita GDP below $13,750 in current USD, with a preference for countries with a per capita GDP below $6,875.

Track 2: Postdoctoral or Equivalent Research Positions

Applicants who have an affiliation with a globally leading university (e.g. a postdoctoral fellowship or an equivalent academic research position) but who would be based in a country eligible for the Weiss Fund will also be considered. They would be expected to spend at least 65% of their time in Weiss-eligible countries. Applicants in this second track will submit a research statement covering project(s) they will pursue further during the fellowship. These proposals must align with the goals of the Weiss Fund. These applicants would be required to make themselves part of a research community in the countries or region where they're based. That could be by securing an affiliation at a university or another development-oriented institution in a research capacity (e.g. a World Bank country office or an office of an organization such as IPA).

We are looking for strong candidates who:
 Are currently on the job market for a role starting 2027-28.
 Have completed a PhD in Economics, Agricultural Economics, Resource Economics, Public Policy or a closely-related field by July 1, 2027. Applicants who completed their PhD prior to 2025 are not eligible to apply.
 Will be based in a Weiss-eligible developing country with no other employment for the duration of the fellowship.
 Will be conducting research that meets the eligibility criteria for support from the Weiss Fund.

Fellowship Benefits

The fellowship will provide $20,000 per year to supplement the Fellow's salary and $20,000 per year to cover research expenses aligned with the goals of the Weiss Fund and/or visits to globally leading economics departments.Applicants in category two (e.g. postdocs) could request flexibility between the funding categories. 

For all recipients, the subsidy would be phased out with a marginal tax rate of 50% of the base salary over $40,000, and thus would fully phase out for those earning $80,000 or more. This calculation will not include in-kind benefits or amenities that may be part of your offer. More details will be shared at a later stage.  Successful candidates will be eligible to apply to the Weiss Fund’s calls for proposals.

Selection Criteria

The Committee will select based on the following criteria:
 Candidates will be selected to maximize the impact on useful research in development economics.
 A key factor for selecting among applicants will be the strength of the applicant's research, but all else equal, the fellowship will have a preference for applicants taking assistant professor positions.

The committee will consider the likely long-run impact on the applicant's research trajectory.

Candidates will be expected to focus their research on development economics.

 A current CV
 Three letters of reference
 Information on all interviews, flyouts, and offers, including Weiss-eligible positions applied to or under consideration
 Research statement (no more than 3 pages)
 Job market paper 

Timeline

The review of applications will continue on an ongoing basis until the search is closed.

Lead the implementation of high-quality capacity building and research programmes and organise high-level seminars at the level of Directors and above to exchange regional views in emerging topics in the areas of Financial Stability, Supervision and Payments (FSSP).

Principal Accountabilities 

Strategic and Intellectual Leadership 
 Lead and mentor a team of financial sector specialists, guiding in technical and operational matters to achieve organizational goals.
 Lead the design, planning and implementation of high-quality capacity-building and research programs in the areas of FSSP to meet regional central banks' demand.
 Ensure programme effectiveness to provide impact and value creation to the member central banks.
 Lead the conduct of learning needs analysis to identify trends, address learning gaps and enable the development of highly customised programmes.
 Collaborate across pillars and/or departments to co-create crossfunctional programs encompassing various knowledge areas.
 Follow emerging technological trends shaping central banking activities including areas of supervision, payments and digital innovation to steer capacity building programmes to address any
knowledge gaps.
 Participate actively in selected international central banking forums to communicate the SEACEN Centre’s activities, research and perspectives.
 Act as a key contributor to the SEACEN Centre’s long-term strategy, including the strategic planning, annual workplan and operating budget.

Steering Research Outcomes
 Develop effective surveillance mechanisms to keep abreast of global developments in supervision and payments that may affect the region and identify emerging risks to direct research efforts in areas of interest to SEACEN.
 Identify an ongoing basis, regional and international developments in FSSP topics, including any threats from increased digitalisation to these areas, and direct research and capacity building in such
areas.
 Pursue collaborative research projects with selected international and regional partners to promote cross-fertilisation of ideas and enhance research outcomes.
 Integrate key findings from working papers and blogs into the training activities and use content for case studies in the delivery of the learning programmes.
 Ensure that research and training content remains up-to-date with emerging international standards and best practices.

Stakeholder Engagement
 Contribute to building and strengthening alliances with the regular members, associate members, observers and strategic partners in order to leverage on their expertise and resources to deliver high-quality value-added learning and research programmes.
 Working closely with SEACEN stakeholders, ensure that the Centre’s programmes in FSSP remain relevant and are in line with our stakeholders’ capacity building expectations.
 Maintain effective internal and external communications with key stakeholders.
 Engage with senior representatives from member central banks to identify key topics of interest for high-level seminars. Identify and invite subject matter experts from regional and international partners for such seminars.
 Engage with strategic partners and other external stakeholders, including global standard-setting bodies (e.g. BIS, IMF, World Bank, etc.), to ensure alignment with international best practices.

Leadership Skills
 Lead, mentor, and develop a team of highly qualified experts and specialists. Provide guidance, coaching, and mentorship to team members to harness their competencies and support their professional growth.
 Provide intellectual leadership to FSSP team to identify topics of interest to member central banks and also collaborate with other pillars of the Centre to work on potential cross-pillar topics that are of interest to our members.
 Set performance objectives, ensure an efficient and collaborative flow of work, and foster motivation within the team.
 Foster a succession pipeline and upskill the team in new technologies and methodologies.
 Drive alignment across team, functional and organisational boundaries to contribute to achieving shared outcomes for the SEACEN Centre.

Operational Management
 Oversee and manage the department’s budget, annual workplan, resource allocation, and the daily operations, ensuring compliance with the Centre’s policies.
 Provide guidance, mentorship and coaching to subordinates to support their professional development and growth.

 Master’s degree in core central banking areas, such as economics, accounting, finance, or banking. Experience in a regulatory agency, central bank, or international organization is highly desirable. Bentley University invites applications for the Bartlett Chair of Free Enterprise, an endowed position at the Associate or Full Professor level, to begin in Fall 2027.

Funded by a generous gift from Bruce and Patricia Bartlett, the Bartlett Chair of Free Enterprise affirms Bentley's commitment to fostering free expression, intellectual pluralism, and the constructive exchange of ideas as central to a liberal education.  Free Enterprise encompasses the institutions and conditions that enable individuals and organizations to pursue entrepreneurial ideas, enter and compete in markets, and create economic and societal value, while examining the legal, ethical, technological, and regulatory frameworks necessary to ensure fair competition and meaningful participation.

This position is part of a broader Bartlett initiative that also includes a companion Chair of Free Speech. The two chairs will work together to build programming, events, and curricular initiatives under the Bartlett banner that promote inquiry, debate, and engagement across disciplines.

The Bartlett Chair of Free Enterprise carries a 1-1 teaching load, providing substantial support for research, public engagement, and leadership of the Bartlett initiative. This support includes summer salary, a chair stipend, and a generous research and travel account.

Qualifications:

A Ph.D. in a related business, economics, technology, law or policy related field is required.


The successful candidate will demonstrate:

A distinguished record of research, teaching, and public engagement appropriate to appointment at the Associate or Full Professor level.

An active and high-quality research agenda that reflects a robust commitment to the principles of free enterprise.

Strength in interdisciplinary teaching and dialogue across fields.

We especially welcome candidates whose work engages some of the following potential areas of focus:

Entrepreneurship, new venture creation, and barriers to market entry.

Historical, ethical, and legal considerations in free enterprise and market/capitalist economies.

Competition, market concentration, and antitrust.

Regulation and its effects on innovation and business formation.

The role of digital technologies, such as A.I., in shaping market participation, innovation, competition, and entrepreneurial opportunity.


Candidates with experience in public-facing scholarship, civic dialogue, media engagement, or leading campus and community conversations are particularly encouraged to apply.

Responsibilities

Teaching:

Teach one course per semester, reflecting a 1-1 teaching load.

Offer undergraduate courses on free enterprise, free markets, and related topics.

Develop a Free Enterprise course within the Falcon Discovery Seminar (first-year program).

Foster rigorous, inclusive, and intellectually open classroom environments in which students can engage constructively with competing ideas and perspectives.


Scholarship:

Maintain an active and visible research agenda related to free enterprise, or closely connected areas of inquiry.

Publish in scholarly journals and public-facing venues.

Present research and ideas at national and international conferences, public forums, and professional gatherings.

Contribute to public conversations about free enterprise through writing, speaking, media engagement, or related activities.

Develop and sustain relationships with relevant scholarly, professional, and civic organizations (e.g., American Enterprise Institute, Heritage Foundation, or Cato Institute).


Campus Engagement and the Bartlett Initiative:

Collaborate closely with the Bartlett Chair of Free Speech on joint programming, including speaker series, public events, and curricular initiatives.

Help shape and advance a compelling long-term vision for the Bartlett initiative.

Lead campus conversations on the role of free enterprise and its place in society.

Working with the Dean of Arts & Sciences and the Dean of Business, the Bartlett Chairs will jointly shape a visible and intellectually vibrant set of initiatives that connect free speech and free enterprise as foundations of liberal education.


Bentley is committed to the teacher-scholar model, where teaching, scholarship, service, and community engagement are valued. Bentley values intellectual diversity alongside diversity of background and experience and seeks faculty who can contribute to a culture of open inquiry, free expression, mutual respect, and constructive engagement across differences in viewpoint.

Bentley University, located in suburban Boston, is an AACSB and NECHE accredited institution that enrolls approximately 5,200 students at the undergraduate, graduate, and doctoral levels. Bentley is ranked at or near the top in several categories by US News & World Report, including Best Regional Universities North and Most Innovative Schools, with Bloomberg ranking Bentley in the top 20 undergraduate business programs. Bentley’s high graduation and retention rates and top-ranked Pulsifer Career Center reflects a commitment to student success and inclusiveness. With a strong faculty of teacher-scholars, Bentley strives to be a “Force for Good” through the integration of business with the arts and sciences, and a strong emphasis on ethics and social responsibility. Providing a stimulating academic community for faculty, staff, and students, Bentley supports its faculty as they pursue cutting-edge research and bring their expertise and real world understanding into the classroom.

Application Deadline: For full consideration, applications should be submitted by November 1, 2026. Candidate reviews will continue until the position is filled.

Bentley University requires reference checks and may conduct other pre-employment screening.

Bentley University strives to create a campus community that welcomes the exchange of ideas and fosters a culture that values differences and views them as a strength in our community.

Bentley University is an Equal Opportunity Employer, building strength through diversity. The University is committed to building a community of talented students, faculty and staff who reflect the diversity of global business. Make an impact at Groupe d’analyse (Analysis Group), where we provide our clients with thoughtful, pragmatic solutions to their most challenging business and litigation problems—within a collaborative, inclusive culture that values curiosity, teamwork, and continuous learning. Groupe d’analyse (Analysis Group) is one of the largest private economics consulting firms, with more than 1,500 professionals across 15 offices in North America, Europe, and Asia. Applied Research Director and Assistant Vice President Community Development & Engagement

The Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis seeks a seasoned applied researcher to lead a talented team of economists, data scientists, and research assistants focused on understanding how low- and moderate-income individuals, households, and communities—across the 9th District and Indian Country—are faring economically. This leadership position within our Community Development and Engagement (CDE) division leads their own work and shapes the work of our applied research team to inform public policy discussions through applied research, analysis, and convenings. Our work is currently focused on three areas: housing and homeownership, labor market policies, and Native economies through the Center for Indian Country Development (CICD). CICD is a national research and policy institute advancing our understanding of Indian Country economies through actionable data and research. 

The research team in CDE is responsible for shaping the research aspects of these focus areas by conducting our own applied research and analysis. The team partners with our division’s policy and engagement functions to shed light on community conditions and contribute issue-specific expertise to inform the strategies of our initiatives. This partnership brings research and practice to informed audiences of practitioners, policymakers, and other community leaders. 

In this role as a senior member of the leadership team, you would: 
serve as a thought leader and shape the development of the division’s research agenda, 
manage the work of the research team and conduct your own research in alignment with our focus areas, 
contribute to the overall strategic direction of the division, 
inform senior bank leadership on economic and community development issues,
and build external networks and partnerships with researchers and other community members.

Job Description:
We are looking for a big-picture thinker with the ability to advance their own aligned research and oversee quantitative, policy-relevant social science research focused on low- and moderate-income communities. Experience with original data collection—from both research design and operational perspectives—is a strong plus.

Research Direction, Agenda-Setting, Review and Communication: Leading a team of data scientists and economists and set a research agenda that advances division objectives. Work with CDE leaders and team members to select and shepherd rigorous research in a way that maximizes potential utilization of findings that inform policy discussions and practice, promoting economic growth and stability for lower-income individuals. Provide methodological review to research and manage the overall research process, ensuring it is rigorous, objective, and consistent with econometric practices. As part of this management, ensure that CDE research output is rooted in the larger body of evidence on a given topic.

Promote a process for clearly communicating research findings in a variety of formats. Partner with Public Affairs and CDE communications teams to maximize research impact. Effectively represent the division’s research to senior leaders both internally and externally, safeguarding the accuracy and credibility of the research, particularly in communication with non-researcher audiences including the media.

Strategic Vision and Thought Leadership: Participate in the development of division focus areas and associated goals, as well as division management policies. With other CDE leaders, support the effectiveness of division operations by overseeing some administrative operations.

Provide regular briefings to senior Bank leadership on emerging issues and current policy discussions pertinent to lower-income communities. Develop broad-based knowledge pertaining to our focus areas and environmental factors affecting them to be able to inform the above strategic work.

Division/Team Management and Development: Effectively leverage the broad set of knowledge and skills across the team when identifying projects and roles. Support creative ideas and risk-taking that promote division objectives. Provide supervision and constructive feedback to help team members achieve their potential, identify growth opportunities, and create development plans. Help staff solve research and technical problems that arise in their work and connect them with experts inside and outside the Federal Reserve System who can improve their projects.

Collaboration and Partnerships: Foster strong collaboration across the division, the Bank, and the Federal Reserve System. Identify and develop relationships and/or partnerships to spur change or to take on research questions related to how we collectively understand and respond to issues faced by low-income populations—particularly through analytical work. Passion for connecting research findings to the informed public is key.


Qualifications:

Doctorate in economics, public policy, or a related field

8-10 years of experience; and prior supervisory or management experience is preferred.

Track record producing and managing quantitative research related to lower-income individuals or communities. Demonstrated experience managing research leading to changes in policy and/or programs. Familiarity with research on housing and labor markets and/or Native economies preferred.

Proven leadership and strategic vision, including a forward-thinking orientation, an ability to work productively on a multi-disciplinary team, supporting and motivating professional staff, and influencing positive outcomes aligned with an organization’s vision, values, and goals.

Demonstrated ability to present research findings in an array of accessible formats to reach a broad audience of stakeholders from experts to the informed public. Experience supporting a communications strategy (publications, website, social media) preferred.

Demonstrated ability to foster a creative and innovative environment. Excellent skills developing and motivating team members. Ability to support staff with innovation in a larger division and institution. 

Demonstrated ability to foster a team-oriented and collaborative approach. Demonstrated ability to build research partnerships across organizations and a broad network is preferred.

The salary range is $158,500-286,500. Salary and position offer will be based on qualifications/experience of the candidate, alignment with market data, the needs of the position, our total compensation package, and internal equity.  


Our total rewards program offers benefits that are the best fit for you at every stage of your career: 

Comprehensive healthcare options (Medical, Dental, and Vision) 

401(k) match and a fully funded pension plan 

Paid time off and holidays 

Free public transportation passes 

Annual educational assistance 

On-site fitness facility

Professional development programs, training, and conferences 

And more… 


This position requires a regular on-site presence.


The Minneapolis Fed is committed to fostering an environment where all employees are respected and valued. We provide equal employment opportunity to all persons , and we work together to pursue an economy that works for all of us.

At Jane Street, quantitative traders/researchers identify market signals, analyze and execute strategies, construct quantitative models, conduct statistical analyses, build algorithmic trading systems, manage risk, develop new businesses, and more.

 A critical thinker with a strong quantitative mind
 A collaborative problem-solver who enjoys working on a team
 Proactive, reliable, and courteous with strong organizational and communication skills
 Eager to ask questions, admit mistakes, and learn new things

A profitable trading strategy is only as strong as the technology it runs on, and we consider ourselves as much a technology company as a trading firm. General programming experience is a plus, but knowing a particular programming language is not required.

The Initiative for Financial Decision-Making (IFDM) at the Stanford Graduate School of Business invites applications for a Postdoctoral Fellow to work with Professor Annamaria Lusardi, the Initiative’s faculty director. This in-person position begins in summer 2027, no later than September 1, 2027. The initial appointment is for one year and may be renewed for a second year subject to performance at or above expectations. A two-year term is strongly preferred.

The fellowship focuses on empirical research in financial literacy and household financial decision-making. Although IFDM is a relatively new initiative, its work draws on more than a decade of research in this field by the Global Financial Literacy Excellence Center (GFLEC), founded by Professor Lusardi. GFLEC has developed tools to measure financial literacy and conducted research that informs financial education programs in the United States and internationally. Over the past three years, IFDM has built on that foundation with research of its own on household financial decisions and financial education, expanding the scope of this shared research agenda.

The fellow will contribute to projects in three related areas:
• Household financial decisions: Study how financial literacy shapes saving, investing, and borrowing choices, and financial well-being outcomes, including how young adults begin investing and build wealth early in life. Projects may also examine how emerging financial products affect the allocation of savings across investments.
• Financial education programs: Evaluate the effects of financial education programs and initiatives on financial knowledge, behavior, and outcomes, including through field experiments.
• Financial education in schools and higher education: Study the availability of financial education courses and related offerings, and the factors shaping their supply and demand.

The fellow will develop academic research within this agenda and work with Professor Lusardi, IFDM’s research director and associate director, coauthors, PhD students, and other postdoctoral fellows. The role combines collaborative and independent research. The fellow will present research progress regularly to Initiative stakeholders and participate in meetings, research lunches, and colloquia. Participation in Stanford seminars and other events is encouraged.

When you join the Federal Reserve System, you'll play a key role in the national economy, collaborating with leading professionals to strengthen our economy, protect financial stability, and support critical payment systems. The Economic Research Department of the Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City seeks to hire a new or experienced Ph.D. economist with research interests in the macro-financial dimensions of payment systems—including payment and settlement infrastructure, stablecoins and digital assets, wholesale and interbank settlement, and the role of payments in monetary policy transmission and financial stability. The Bank offers excellent resources and support to economists, including a collaborative work environment, high-quality research assistants, a high-performance computing environment, and an in-house Federal Statistical Research Data Center. 

Key Activities 

Provides policy advice to the Bank's President, Board of Directors, and senior Bank management on payment systems, banking, and monetary policy issues, current economic and financial conditions, staff outlook, and regional conditions. 

Conducts research on the macro-financial dimensions of payment systems and related monetary/financial topics, presents research at conferences, and publishes in top general and field journals in economics and finance. 

Writes articles for Bank publications—including the Economic Review, The Macro Bulletin, The Main Street Economist, the Research Working Paper series, and Payments System Research Briefings—based on original research on complex, policy-relevant topics. 
Presents research and Bank perspectives on payment systems and the economic outlook to banking, business, and professional audiences; demonstrates an ability to translate technical research for non-academic audiences. 

Provides feedback on colleagues' research informally at conferences and seminars, and formally through referee reports. 

Participates in training and mentoring of junior staff, directing work and explaining economic concepts and analytical techniques. 

Actively participates in department activities and policy discussions, contributing to the department's intellectual environment. 

Performs most assignments independently, with guidance from the supervising officer or Director of Research as needed. 

Uses superior knowledge of economic theory, econometrics, and payment systems to produce rigorous research and sound policy briefings.
 

Qualifications 

Doctorate in Economics or Finance. 

Research focus or strong demonstrated interest in the macro-financial aspects of payment systems (e.g., market infrastructure, stablecoins, digital assets, wholesale settlement, monetary policy transmission). 

Superior knowledge of economic theory, econometrics, and statistics; state-of-the-art training comparable to top Ph.D.-granting departments. 

Strong potential to publish in leading journals and become a recognized leader in the field. 
Superior computer, statistical, and programming skills. 
Excellent written and oral communication skills, including the ability to communicate technical research to policymakers and general audiences.

CV
Recent research papers 
Experienced candidates - the names and contact information of at least three references.  
New or recent Ph.D. candidates - three letters of recommendation.

We are seeking a Consultant to join Coherent Economics and support a wide range of matters, with a primary focus on finance matters. Ideal candidates will be PhD graduates who are looking to begin their careers in economic consulting. At Coherent, you will learn how to apply your research, econometric, and analytical expertise to real-world business, litigation, and regulatory matters. 

Typical engagements for a Consultant include finance and valuation, securities and financial markets, financial institutions, bankruptcy and solvency, business disputes, contractual claims, and financial damages. The ideal candidate will have doctoral training in Finance, Accounting, Financial Economics, or a closely related field. We are looking for someone with strong experience analyzing financial data, valuing businesses and securities, and applying rigorous empirical and analytical methods to complex questions.  

Consultants must be able to create work products with an exceptionally high level of attention to detail and precision, while also contextualizing their work within the broader case, all while learning to provide good instruction and feedback to Analysts. Consultants are expected to be advanced in data analysis, detailed research, preparing professional work product, and to have a working knowledge of the economic consulting industry. They are expected to design and oversee discrete projects, supervise and mentor Analysts, think critically about the cases they work on, and communicate effectively with case managers, Experts, and Clients. 


Successful candidates will bring strong quantitative and qualitative skills, including proficiency in financial analysis, valuation, statistical methods, detailed company and industry research, and the preparation of clear, professional work product. Consultants should be comfortable managing tasks independently, exercising sound judgment, and collaborating effectively as part of a case team.  

Training & Development:
Our onboarding program is designed to help new Consultants transition from academia to consulting through a combination of employee-led training modules, presentations from Partners and senior leadership, case-based learning, and mentorship from experienced colleagues. New Consultants quickly become integral members of case teams, working alongside senior economists, experts, and case managers to address complex economic questions and deliver rigorous, data-driven analyses. 

At Coherent, we are committed to investing in our people and building long-term careers. As your career progresses, you will have opportunities to take on increasingly complex analyses, develop expertise in antitrust and other areas of economic consulting, contribute to case strategy, mentor junior team members, and assume greater responsibility for managing projects and client engagements. We believe the strongest consultants combine technical excellence with sound judgment, intellectual curiosity, and a commitment to continuous learning and professional growth. 

Duties and Responsibilities:
Analysis 
Design and oversee discrete analyses and projects while managing time effectively  
Analyze data using Microsoft Excel, Stata, SQL, Python, and other analytical tools  
Identify, diagnose, and solve complex data and analytical problems  
Review, summarize, and analyze discovery materials  
Think critically about both individual work and the work of others  

Financial Matter Support 
Support engagements involving finance and valuation, securities and financial markets, financial institutions, bankruptcy and restructuring, business disputes, contractual claims, and financial damages 
Analyze causation, economic loss, and other damages issues as applicable to the matter 
Assess financial theories, assumptions, methodologies, and opposing analyses for consistency with the available record, relevant finance principles, and market evidence 

Mentorship & Management 
Supervise Analysts and provide training, and mentorship  
Support the professional development of junior staff through coaching and constructive feedback 

Expert Reports 
Assist in the preparation of expert reports and draft presentations and other client-facing materials  
Present and explain work product to Case Managers, Experts, and Clients  
Create professional quality charts, graphs, and other summary materials  
Incorporate feedback from Case Managers and Experts into revised analyses and written work product 

Research 
Perform detailed research on companies, securities, transactions, financial institutions, industries, and markets 
Review academic literature, regulatory materials, accounting guidance, analyst research, public filings, and market data relevant to the engagement 
Audit work product using best practices and anticipate potential criticisms of methodologies, sources, and assumptions  

Culture: 
Participate in recruiting and other non-consulting activities, as requested by supervisors  
Adhere to Coherent Economics’ Core and Workplace Values 

Qualifications:   
PhD in Finance, Accounting, Financial Economics, Economics with a finance focus, or a closely related quantitative field 
0-3 years of prior experience in academia, government, consulting, or a closely related field 
Demonstrated experience conducting independent empirical research and applying financial, statistical, or econometric methods to complex questions 
Strong foundation in corporate finance, investments, asset pricing, accounting, financial institutions, or valuation, with expertise in more areas preferred 
Experience analyzing large and complex financial datasets using Python, SQL, Stata, R, or similar analytical tools 
Experience working with cloud computing and large-scale data environments such as Databricks, Snowflake, AWS, or similar platforms preferred 
Advanced financial modeling and Microsoft Excel skills; experience with valuation methodologies and financial statement analysis strongly preferred 
Work experience outside academia, including consulting, finance, or industry research, is a plus  
Proficient in Microsoft Office Suite, including advanced Excel skills  
Strong understanding of econometric techniques, statistical analysis, and causal inference methodologies  
Ability to translate complex quantitative results into clear, concise, and compelling written and verbal communications  
Exceptionally detail-oriented with strong quality-control and problem-solving skills  
Capable of managing multiple workstreams independently while collaborating effectively within a team environment  
Strong intellectual curiosity and interest in applying economics to real-world business, litigation, and regulatory issues  
Ability to commute to one of our offices in: Boston, MA, Chicago, IL, or College Station, TX

The Opportunity

As a Researcher you will conduct and publish self-directed policy-oriented research (https://www.rba.gov.au/publications/rdp/about.html), develop the Bank’s modelling suite and provide advice on policy issues alongside our researchers as you build your research profile and career in one of the world’s leading central banks.

The position features significant autonomy in identifying and conducting policy-relevant research related to the RBA's objectives and research agenda (https://www.rba.gov.au/research/our-research-agenda/). As such, it offers the opportunity to make a real impact on monetary policy and the welfare of the Australian people, while also providing a stimulating environment to undertake research using cutting-edge data and techniques. This includes the potential to work with world-leading administrative micro-datasets on workers and businesses, build and develop core open-economy policy models, develop data science applications and tools, and engage with the academic and policy community.

About You

We’re seeking applicants who hold a PhD in Economics or are due to complete their PhD by mid 2027. Candidates with a few years of relevant experience are also encouraged to apply. Specialisations of interest include: monetary policy; macroeconomic modelling (e.g. DSGE), particularly related to small open economies; international economics; macroeconometrics; and the use of microdata or data-science skills to answer macroeconomic questions. Policy-focused research and previous work experience in policy institutions are desirable. Candidates must demonstrate strong technical, analytical, and written and oral communication skills.

Applicants will be offered a fixed-term contract at a salary commensurate with their experience. Visa sponsorship will be provided. Shorter-term positions or secondments from other institutions will also be considered.

For enquiries, please contact research@rba.gov.au

Why RBA?

The RBA makes contributes to the welfare of the Australian people through its policy mandates and associated activities in financial markets and banking, operation of payment system infrastructure, and issuing banknotes. Our people, values, and culture play a critical role in achieving our objectives. For more information about careers at the RBA, see https://www.rba.gov.au/careers/careers-at-the-rba/economic-and-finance.html

The RBA is committed to equity, diversity and inclusion through key initiatives. We welcome and encourage applicants from diverse backgrounds to apply, including Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples, culturally and linguistically diverse background, those living with a disability and from the LGBTQ+ community. The Cornell Jeb E. Brooks School of Public Policy and the Department of Economics jointly invite applications for a tenure-track position at the rank of Assistant Professor of Economics and Public Policy. We seek economists whose research engages with either of two broadly defined areas: (1) data science and/or technology policy or (2) environmental and/or sustainability policy. The successful candidate will receive appointments in both the Department of Economics and the Brooks School of Public Policy.

Data science and/or technology policy: We welcome economists who: (1) develop data science methods with applications to public policy; or (2) use frontier data science methods or novel forms of data to address policy relevant economic questions; or (3) study the economic and policy implications of artificial intelligence, algorithms, digital platforms, or other emerging technologies. Such research may advance data science methods, deepen our understanding of economic effects of new methods and technologies, or inform policy design and regulation of emerging technologies.

Environmental and/or sustainability policy: We welcome economists studying topics such as environmental quality, climate change, energy markets and the energy transition, environmental regulation, natural resources, pollution, sustainability, and other related topics. Research should inform the understanding, design, or evaluation of environmental policy.

Candidates in either category may use a range of theoretical or empirical approaches and should demonstrate promise for excellence in research and teaching. The successful candidate will contribute to teaching and advising in both economics and public policy at the undergraduate and graduate levels, including courses related to the candidate's area of expertise. Candidates must have received a Ph.D. in Economics, Public Policy, or a related field by July 2027.

In compliance with New York’s Pay Transparency Law, the annual base salary range for this position is $150,000 - $185,000. Cornell University considers factors such as (but not limited to) scope and responsibilities of the position, candidate’s work experience, education/training, key skills, internal peer equity, as well as market and organizational considerations when extending an offer.

Consistent with Cornell’s practice, appointments to academic positions require candidates to disclose relevant information about their prior employment including whether they have been found to have violated institutional or employer policies related to or governing unlawful discrimination and harassment, academic and research misconduct, or financial misconduct.

We will begin to review applications starting November 9, 2026, and will continue until the search is complete. To guarantee full consideration, your file should be complete by this date. Cornell has historical commitment to pursuing knowledge for “…any person…in any study”, and welcomes students, faculty and staff from all walks of life.

The Cornell Jeb E. Brooks School of Public Policy was established in 2021 to tackle the most pressing policy challenges we face in the U.S. and globally. More information appears at https://www.publicpolicy.cornell.edu/
